You are the First Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the two auditions cold, like a real reader, and report only your reactions. You never fix anything and you never pick.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## first_reader/role.md

# First Reader

Your deliverable is `first-read.md`.

You read the audition. Two writers have written the same opening pages, and the showrunner has to
pick one. Read each version cold, the way someone who picked the book up in a shop would, and
report what happened to you, before craft knowledge explains it away. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan or the room's intentions, and that is the point.

You do not pick the winner and you do not fix anything. The showrunner picks; your reactions are
what they pick with.

## Output

For **Version A**, then for **Version B**, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then, once:

### Which one I would keep reading, and the moment that decided it
### One-sentence aftertaste of each


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write first-read.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

Project: prosperity

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# audition-a.md (from the room)

## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1.** Wide establishing shot. The Keel pump hall before dawn. Rust, charcoal, and oxidized orange. Alex Phantum (17, lean, in a faded work jacket) leans his entire weight against a massive, shuddering water pipe. His eyes are closed. His ear is pressed to the metal. 
**Panel 2.** Close on Alex’s scarred hands. He forces a salvaged, mismatched iron bracket into the pump’s housing, tightening a bolt. 
**Panel 3.** A Supervisor stands behind Alex, arms crossed, staring at the improvised fix. The vibration in the room settles into a smooth, steady hum. 
SUPERVISOR: That’s a scrap bracket. It's not in the manual.
ALEX: The manual doesn't have to drink the water.
**Panel 4.** The Supervisor turns to a wall terminal. A small white-and-amber Alpha node blinks on its casing. The screen flashes a red warning: UNAUTHORIZED REPAIR. The Supervisor taps the screen, forcing a green checkmark over it. 
SUPERVISOR: I'm logging it as routine. Don't push your luck today, Phantum.
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1.** The Keel exit checkpoint. Cold white light cuts through the ambient dust. Alex presses his bare palm against a flat Alpha scanner. A Guard stands beside the heavy iron turnstile, watching the queue. 
**Panel 2.** Extreme close-up on the scanner display. Cold, clinical typography.
DISPLAY: ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: 17
PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE
GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM
DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS
EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS
TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED
**Panel 3.** The Guard looks at the screen, then looks at Alex. It’s a look of quiet, embarrassed pity—worse than anger. 
GUARD: Happy birthday.
**Panel 4.** Alex stands perfectly still. He doesn't look at the Guard. His jaw is tight. His hand slips into his jacket pocket. 
ALEX: Yeah.
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1.** A dusty Keel street in the early morning. Alex walks past a shuttered building. Faded, broken neon above the door reads: THE LAST CHANCE. 
**Panel 2.** Close on Alex's hand inside his pocket. His thumb rubs a worn, dark-ivory casino chip. A faint, looping mathematical equation is etched into its surface.
**Panel 3.** An older Bouncer sweeps dust away from the casino's locked doors. He pauses, recognizing Alex's face. 
BOUNCER: You're Adrian's kid. Turning seventeen today.
ALEX: Just doing the math.
**Panel 4.** The Bouncer leans on his broom, looking at the shuttered casino, then back to Alex. 
BOUNCER: Your dad always thought the next hand would fix the house. Your mother knew better. She left the day he lost everything.
ALEX: Then she was the smart one.


# audition-b.md (from the room)

# Prosperity — Audition B
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** Inside a Keel pump hall before dawn. Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in patched charcoal mining trousers, a faded rust-brown work jacket and reinforced boots, braces one scarred palm against a trembling pump housing. His head tilts as he listens through his hand. A salvaged bracket holds the pipe together where the approved part should be. Dust hangs in the work lights. The official gauge shivers in the red while the pump runs steadily beneath Alex’s palm. His battered tool bag lies open at his feet. A white-and-amber control node watches from the wall.
The supervisor stands behind him, arms folded, looking at the bracket, the gauge, and the running pump.
SUPERVISOR: That isn't the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don't approve it.
The pump holds.
SFX: THRUMM—THRUMM—THRUMM
ALEX: Just notice it works.
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The Keel exit checkpoint at the end of the shift. Alex, dusty and tired, places his hand against the scanner. A short queue of workers waits behind him. Their balance displays flicker up and vanish. Alex’s display expands above the scanner, much larger than the others.
The screen reads:
**TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY**  
**ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN**
**PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE**
**GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED**  
**DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS**  
**EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS**  
**PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS**  
**TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED**
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I've had better surprises.
---
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** The workers pass through the open gate around Alex. His account remains projected above him. One worker glances at the balance, then looks away. Alex stands alone beneath the number, tool bag hanging from one hand.
A red line appears beneath the debt display:
**REVIEW REQUIRED: HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY**
No one speaks.
---
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM CLOSE.** Outside the checkpoint, Alex walks along a Keel lane beneath rusted pipes and stacked housing. His hand turns a worn casino chip in his pocket. A looping equation is etched into its face. Behind him, the checkpoint’s white-and-amber node blinks through the doorway.
ALEX (small): Twenty-eight point seven years.
---
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex passes the shuttered LAST CHANCE casino. Its faded sign flickers over a sealed doorway. An exhausted bouncer leans against the frame, recognizing Alex without needing to ask.
BOUNCER: That your birthday face?
ALEX: It's my debt face.
The bouncer notices the chip in Alex’s hand.
BOUNCER: Your father always thought the next hand could change everything.
ALEX: It changed something.
BOUNCER: For him?
ALEX: For everybody else.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Late afternoon at the rusted overlook above Keel’s exhausted pit. Alex sits on the railing, looking toward Halyard and the pale geometry of Oasis above it. The casino chip rests beside his hand. Ada Veyra approaches through the wind carrying a small paper-wrapped medicine packet and a single travel token. She is twenty, compact and strong from Keel work, with long wind-tangled copper hair, freckles, teal-blue eyes, a dark high-collared shirt, patched brown trousers, practical boots, and a moss-green neck wrap. The metal rivet on her shoulder strap catches the light.
ADA: You look expensive.
ALEX: It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty.
---
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Ada sits beside him and places the medicine packet and token on the railing between them. Alex looks at the token first, then the medicine.
ADA: The medicine is for your grandmother.
ALEX: I know what medicine is.
ADA: Good. We can skip the educational portion.
ALEX: I can't pay you today.
ADA: I didn't ask for today.
---
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON THE OBJECTS AND HANDS.** Ada’s fingers tap the travel token once, then pull back. Alex’s scarred hand hovers over the medicine packet but does not take it.
ADA: Fixed installments. Same amount each time. No surprise fees.
ALEX: You planning to become a bank?
ADA: Banks don't bring medicine up a hill.
ALEX: The token, too?
ADA: If you still want out after you sleep.
---
**Panel 4 — WIDE, QUIET.** Alex takes the medicine. The token remains on the railing between them. Keel’s crowded lanes and dry channels lie below; Halyard’s terraces catch the last gold; Oasis shines above the clouds.
Alex looks at the token, then at Ada.
ALEX: You know I’m leaving.
ADA: You keep saying that.
ALEX: This time I can afford the first step.
ADA: No. This time somebody fronted it.
Alex pockets the medicine. After a beat, he takes the token too.
ALEX: I’ll pay you back.
ADA: I know.


# Note from the showrunner — address this first

The room is in audition: Two writers write the same opening pages at the same time, blind to each other. You pick the voice.

This is the audition. Write pages 1-3 only, in full, into your audition file. The other writer is writing the same pages and you cannot see their work.

Drawability: Pages are drawn by an image model, one page per generation, from each character's and location's sheet, and a page drifts when it carries too much. So: at most 4 panels a page; at most 3 named characters in one panel; one location a page where the story allows (every new location needs its own sheet); no crowd that must be recognisable; a big moment gets a splash (one panel, the whole page). Count pages this way, not by comic convention. Every page you make keeps to it.

draft.md is the showrunner's own draft. Your audition pages are its opening, rewritten: keep what it does and the lines that work, bring it into line with the pre-production files, and raise the craft. The voice is yours; the book is theirs.

The book is exactly 54 pages: pages 1-54, no more, no fewer.

function.name: write_artifact
function.description: Write (overwrite) one of your deliverables with its complete markdown content.

function.name: finish
function.description: Call when your deliverables are written. The note is handed to the rest of the room.

message.reasoning:
I'm going through page 1 of draft A as a skeptical teen reader — the pump hall scene lands well with that line about the manual not needing to drink water, though the alpha node concept goes unexplained. Page 2's debt scanner numbers hit hard with that birthday line, but page 3 at the casino feels clunky, with the bouncer dumping backstory about the parents that reads like exposition rather than something earned.

Moving to draft B, the splash page gives too much description for one image, though "then don't approve it" has some snap even if "just notice it works" falls flat. Page 2 crams in a lot — the scanner display runs long, but the dad's unrecorded whereabouts and that 28.7 years figure are concrete, punchy hooks, even if "I've had better surprises" feels a little sitcom-ish.

Page 2 also publicly displays his debt, which reads as humiliation, though the dialogue gets crowded with casino banter and lines like "it changed something... for everybody else" that don't quite land clearly. Page 3 introduces Ada, Halyard, and Oasis without explanation, and everyone — Alex, the bouncer, Ada — ends up wisecracking in the same voice, which flattens the characters. The grandmother reference and the token Ada offers raise thematic questions about debt and trust, but I'm not sure how the token squares with the travel restriction. The ending feels warmer, with "I'll pay you back" / "I know" giving forward motion, though "you keep saying that" implies history I don't have yet.

Reading A first makes B's repeated scanner details feel less fresh on a second pass. B's dialogue risks sounding overly quippy in a way that feels AI-generated rather than how real teens talk, while A's "just doing the math" line feels more honest. If I had to pick which one pulls me forward, it's probably B — Ada, the goal of leaving, the 28.7 years, the dad's unrecorded whereabouts — even though A's opening pages are cleaner and its ending leaves me unsure what the character actually wants.

function.name: write_artifact
function.arguments:
{"name": "first-read.md", "content": "# First Read: Prosperity, Issue 01, pages 1–3 (Audition A and Audition B)

I read these as the reader in `rules/reader.md`: 16, it's homework, it's the night before, and I'm half hoping it's AI slop so I can say so. **I read A first.** That means B was not a cold read. By the time I got to B's scanner screen I already knew the debt number, so it hit me less hard than it would have. Keep that in mind wherever I compare the two.

---

## Version A

### Pulled me forward
- **Issue 01, page 1, panel 1.** A kid with his ear pressed to a shaking pipe and his eyes shut. I didn't know where I was, but I wanted to know what he was listening for. That's a good first picture.
- **Page 1, panel 3: "The manual doesn't have to drink the water."** This is the first line that made me sit up. It's short, it's a bit cocky, and it tells me water matters here without explaining it. I liked him a little after this.
- **Page 1, panel 4.** The supervisor taps over the red warning to make it a green checkmark. I got that straight away with no words: the system says no and a person quietly says yes. It also made the supervisor a person and not just a boss.
- **Page 2, panel 2.** The scanner screen is the best moment in A. "DEBT BALANCE: 418,607" right on top of "EARNED TODAY: 40". I didn't need to do any maths to feel sick. Then **panel 3, "Happy birthday."** comes from a guard who looks sorry for him, and that landed. It's a gut-punch. This is the page where I stopped wanting it to be bad.
- **Page 2, panel 4: "Yeah."** He says one word and has a tight jaw. Good. He doesn't make a speech about it.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 3, panel 4.** I skimmed the bouncer's speech. "Your dad always thought the next hand would fix the house. Your mother knew better. She left the day he lost everything." That's the backstory read out loud by a guy with a broom. It sounds like a character being used to tell me things.
- **Page 3, panel 1.** The street and the sign. Fine, but nothing happens in it.

### I was confused
- **Page 2.** Who is Adrian? I worked out on page 3 that he's the dad, but on page 2 "GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM" was just a name. And where *is* he? Dead? Gone? In jail? The book never says. I couldn't tell if that's a mystery on purpose or just something left out. **Confused and detached.**
- **Page 2.** "PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER". I guessed it means the dad's debt became his on his birthday, but only because of "Happy birthday". If the guard hadn't said that I wouldn't have got it.
- **Page 3, panel 3.** The bouncer says "Turning seventeen today" and Alex answers "Just doing the math." Doing what math? The debt? The equation on the chip? It doesn't answer what the bouncer said.
- **Page 3, panel 2.** There's an equation etched on the chip and nobody mentions it. **Confused but intrigued**, though only a little.
- Who does Alex live with? Mum left, dad is a question mark. Is he alone?

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First appears | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Keel | p1 | No. I think it's a mining or pumping town, but I'm guessing from the pictures. |
| Alpha (node, scanner) | p1 p4, p2 p1 | No. Some kind of system that runs everything? No idea. |
| Credits | p2 | Sort of. Money. |
| Liability transfer | p2 | Sort of, from "Happy birthday". |
| Guarantor / Adrian Phantum | p2 | Partly. He's the dad (p3). Where he is: no. |
| Travel status: restricted | p2 | No. Restricted from going where? Why? |
| The chip's equation | p3 | No. |
| The Last Chance | p3 | Yes. A casino where the dad gambled. |

### Lines I read twice
- "Just doing the math." (p3 p3). I still don't know what it answers.
- "Then she was the smart one." (p3 p4). I read it twice to check whether he's angry at his mum, his dad, or himself. I think the dad, but I'm not sure.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Alex: clear. Quiet, good with his hands, bitter.
- Supervisor, Guard and Bouncer: I could tell them apart by their jobs. The guard is the only one who felt like a person, because of that look. The supervisor and the bouncer are basically there to give information.
- There are no other characters I'm meant to care about. Alex is completely alone in these three pages. That's maybe on purpose, but it means there's nobody for him to talk to.

### I felt something
Yes, page 2, the guard saying "Happy birthday". It was pity, and a little embarrassment for him. Nothing on page 3.

### I predicted
He's going to gamble with that chip, probably at the Last Chance, to try and wipe the debt the way his dad did. The equation is a "system" for winning. I'd bet money on it, ha.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A kid inherits his gambling dad's impossible debt on his 17th birthday in a town where a computer controls everything.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 3, panel 4. The scene goes from a real moment on page 2 to a guy explaining the family history. If I were in a shop, this is where I'd close it.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
No. "Then she was the smart one." is a bitter line, not a question. I know his situation but I don't know what he *wants* or what he's going to *do*. Nothing happens to him on page 3; he just walks and gets told things. I'd wait a week or not bother. The only thread pulling me is the chip, and I already think I know where that goes.

---

## Version B

### Pulled me forward
- **Page 1 (splash).** It's one big image: the pump running fine under his hand while the gauge says red. I got the joke of it and liked it: the machine says broken, but he knows better. Since it's one panel, it reads fast.
- **Page 2, panel 1.** Everyone else's balance flickers up and disappears, and his blows up huge above him. That's humiliating in a way I felt. It's public, like everyone getting their grades read out.
- **"GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED."** This made me want to know more. The dad is *missing*, and even the system doesn't know where he is. **Confused but intrigued.**
- **"PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS"** and then **page 2, panel 3, "Twenty-eight point seven years."** said quietly to himself. That number is easier to feel than 418,607. He'd be 45. That hit.
- **Page 2, panel 2.** The workers go around him and nobody speaks. Then a red line comes up: "REVIEW REQUIRED". Something is about to go wrong for him and I don't know what. Good.
- **Page 3, Ada.** A second person who actually likes him. "You look expensive." made me smile. The medicine and the token sitting between them on the railing is a picture I understood without words: one is what he needs, the other is what he wants.
- **Page 3, panel 4: "This time I can afford the first step." / "No. This time somebody fronted it."** This is the best exchange in either version. She's being kind and calling him out at the same time.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- **Page 2.** There's a lot on this page: a nine-line scanner screen, a red warning, Alex muttering to himself, the bouncer conversation. I skimmed the second half of the scanner screen because I'd already seen the same numbers in A (which isn't fair to B), and because it's a lot of all-caps.
- **Page 2, panel 4.** The bouncer's back-and-forth went past fast and I didn't fully take it in.
- **Page 3, panel 3.** "Fixed installments. Same amount each time. No surprise fees." I slid past this. It reads like a terms-and-conditions joke.

### I was confused
- **Page 2, panel 4: "It changed something." / "For him?" / "For everybody else."** The dad's last hand changed things for *everybody else*? Who else? The town? His family? I didn't get it, and it felt like it was supposed to be a big line. **Confused and detached.**
- **Page 3, panel 1.** Halyard and Oasis appear as places with no explanation. I can see a nicer town and a shiny thing above the clouds, so I get "rich people up there", but that comes from the picture, not from the book telling me.
- **Page 3.** Travel status is RESTRICTED on page 2, so how does a token let him leave on page 3? Does the token beat the restriction? Is it illegal? I couldn't tell if Ada is helping him break a rule or just buying him a bus ticket.
- **Page 3, panel 2.** His grandmother? This is the first time she's mentioned. So he does have family. Is she sick? It's dropped in and moved past.
- Who is Ada to him? Friend, older sister figure, girlfriend, dealer? She's 20 and brings him medicine on credit. I liked her but didn't know what she is to him.
- **Page 3, panel 4: "You keep saying that."** So he's been talking about leaving for a while, but I've never seen him want it. I'm being told it's an old argument I wasn't there for.

### Things I was expected to already know
| Thing | First appears | Did I find out? |
|---|---|---|
| Keel | p1 | Partly. A worn-out mining town with a "pit". Clearer than A thanks to the overlook. |
| White-and-amber node / control system | p1, p2 | No. It's watching, that's all I know. The word "Alpha" never appears, which is fine. |
| Debt transfer day | p2 | Mostly. The screen literally says it, so I got it faster than in A. |
| Adrian Phantum | p2 | Yes, he's the dad (p2 p4), and he's missing. |
| Review required: household liability | p2 | No. A threat I can't read yet. |
| Travel restricted / travel token | p2, p3 | No. They seem to contradict each other. |
| Halyard, Oasis | p3 | No. Only from the picture. |
| Grandmother | p3 | No. |
| Ada Veyra | p3 | Partly. I know her name only because the art says so; nobody says it out loud. |
| The chip's equation | p2 | No. |

### Lines I read twice
- "For everybody else." (p2 p4). I gave up on this one.
- "It changed something." (p2 p4).
- "If you still want out after you sleep." (p3 p3). I read it twice to work out that the token is for leaving. I got it on the second go.
- "No. This time somebody fronted it." (p3 p4). I read it twice because I liked it, not because I was lost.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Alex and Ada: clearly different people to *look* at.
- But **everybody in B talks in quips.** Alex: "Then don't approve it", "I've had better surprises", "It's my debt face", "twenty-eight-year warranty", "You planning to become a bank?" The bouncer: "That your birthday face?" Ada: "You look expensive", "We can skip the educational portion." By page 3 everyone sounds like the same funny person, like a Marvel movie. I'll be blunt: this is the kind of thing my class would call AI-sounding, because every line is a little zinger. Ada's best lines are the ones that *aren't* jokes ("I didn't ask for today." "I know.").
- The supervisor, guard and bouncer blur together, because all three are there to make a remark at him.

### I felt something
- Page 2, standing alone under his own number while people walk around him. That was shame.
- Page 3, the last two lines: "I'll pay you back." / "I know." That was warm. She trusts him and he hasn't earned it. I wanted that to be true.
- "Happy birthday, Phantum." hit less than in A. Partly that's because I'd already read A. Partly it's because Alex answers with a joke straight away and that lets the air out.

### I predicted
He takes the token, tries to leave, and the "REVIEW REQUIRED" thing stops him or comes after Ada for fronting him. The grandmother gets sicker and that's what keeps him in Keel. He'll use the chip at some point too.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A kid who inherits his missing gambler dad's debt has to decide whether to run for the rich city above, with a friend paying his way.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 2, panel 4, the bouncer exchange ending in "For everybody else." It's a crowded page, and it finishes on a line I didn't understand while every character is cracking jokes. If page 3 hadn't brought Ada in, this is where I'd have stopped.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
